Lastly, the City’s appeal claims the original DM denying its late RPA was misfiled, and that the DM in its file referenced another applicant. The City argues these errors delayed its ability to track its submission. However, these errors occurred after the initial RPA deadline of June 20, 2025, and did not affect the City’s ability to timely submit its RPA. The City also received a corrected DM and was given time to appeal.

Conclusion

The City did not submit the RPA within the RPA submission deadline and did not demonstrate extenuating circumstances beyond its or the Recipient’s control to justify extending the deadline. Therefore, this appeal is denied.

1. ^ [...] Second Appeal

The City submitted its second appeal of the denial of its late RPA request, reiterating its first appeal arguments. The City details its contacts with the Recipient from April 23 to 25, 2026, prior to submitting its initial claim and documentation, and its receipt of denial determinations involving other unrelated applicants and projects. It states that electric correspondence failures and possible clerical errors apparently played a part in its late RPA submission and FEMA’s denial. On June 24, 2026, the Recipient transmitted the City’s second appeal. The Recipient states it does not support the second appeal, reiterating the same reasons it provided with transmission of the City’s first appeal.

Discussion [...] On May 12, 2026, the FEMA Region 7 Regional Administrator (RA) denied the appeal. FEMA found that the City submitted its RPA untimely, 108 days after the June 20, 2025 deadline. FEMA determined that the City’s cited technical communications issues did not constitute extenuating circumstances beyond the City’s or Recipient’s control to justify an extension of the RPA submission deadline. FEMA also noted that the City did not provide documentation of its attempt to email the Recipient before the deadline.

Implementing this provision, Title 44 of the Code of Federal Regulations (C.F.R.) § 206.206(c) (2016) and FEMA policy require that applicants submit appeals within 60 calendar days of receiving notice of the action that is being appealed. results.title: Read Your FEMA Letter Carefully | FEMA.gov
results.content:
Appealing FEMA’s Decision

If you disagree with FEMA's decision or the amount of money provided, you can submit an appeal letter and documents supporting your claim, such as a contractor's estimate for home repairs. You have 60 days from the date of your letter to appeal.

At the end of your FEMA letter, look for an appeal form that can be used to send us additional information about your situation. This form can help make sure you have the information FEMA needs and gives you space to explain why you need help. [...] It is important to read the letter carefully because it will include the amount of money FEMA may provide and information on the appropriate use of that money. The letter will also explain your application status and advise what you need to do to appeal if you disagree with the decision.

Often, you only need to send additional information or supporting documentation for FEMA to continue reviewing your application for financial assistance. Examples of missing documentation may include:

For more information on understanding your FEMA letter, please visit FEMA.gov/letter.

Appealing FEMA’s Decision [...] Appeals must be postmarked within 60 days of the date noted on your FEMA letter. Appeal letters and supporting documents may be uploaded to your personal FEMA online account. To set up an account, visit DisasterAssistance.gov and follow the directions. You can also find step-by-step instructions for creating an account and uploading documents by visiting DisasterAssistance.gov: A Guide for Survivors.

Other ways to submit documents include:

All documents you send to FEMA as part of your appeal should include your

If you choose to have a third party submit an appeal on your behalf, include a statement signed by you, authorizing the third party to appeal a decision on your behalf, unless those documents are already on file.

results.title: Disaster Assistance Center Opens October 1 | FEMA.gov
results.content:
What FEMA assistance may provide: FEMA helps with basic, essential needs not covered by insurance or other sources. Depending on individual circumstances, assistance may include a grant to help with certain disaster-related losses and may help with basic repairs to make a primary residence safe, sanitary, and functional. [FEMA assistance is not a replacement for insurance and is not able to restore all losses.]

Next steps: After applying, a FEMA staff person and an Oglala Sioux Tribal Guide will call you to make an appointment to come to your home to look at your damages, usually within a week or two of your application. Please answer the call and schedule your visit as soon as possible. This important step must be completed before assistance is approved.
